content: Adverse events involving joints and/or surrounding tissues have been observed. In preclinical studies, oral administration of ciprofloxacin caused lameness in immature dogs. Histopathological examination of the weight-bearing joints in these dogs revealed permanent cartilage lesions. Other quinolone-class drugs have also been shown to cause cartilage erosions in weight-bearing joints and other signs of arthropathy in immature animals across various species. Some fluoroquinolones, including ciprofloxacin, have been associated with prolongation of the QT interval on electrocardiograms and, in rare cases, arrhythmias. Rare cases of torsade de pointes have been reported spontaneously during postmarketing surveillance in patients receiving fluoroquinolones, including ciprofloxacin. Ciprofloxacin should be avoided in patients with known QT interval prolongation, risk factors for QT prolongation or torsade de pointes (e.g., congenital long QT syndrome, uncorrected electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, and cardiac diseases such as heart failure, myocardial infarction, or bradycardia), and in patients receiving Class IA antiarrhythmic agents (e.g., quinidine, procainamide) or Class III antiarrhythmic agents (e.g., amiodarone, sotalol), tricyclic antidepressants, macrolides, or antipsychotics. Elderly patients may also be more susceptible to drug-associated effects on the QT interval. Ciprofloxacin is an inhibitor of the hepatic CYP1A2 enzyme pathway. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with drugs primarily metabolized by CYP1A2 (e.g., theophylline, methylxanthines, caffeine, tizanidine, ropinirole, clozapine, olanzapine) results in increased plasma concentrations of the co-administered drug, potentially leading to clinically significant pharmacodynamic side effects. Ciprofloxacin has not been shown to be effective in the treatment of syphilis. The use of antimicrobial agents in high doses for short periods to treat gonorrhea may mask or delay the symptoms of incubating syphilis. All patients with gonorrhea should undergo serologic testing for syphilis at the time of diagnosis. Patients treated with ciprofloxacin should have a follow-up serologic test for syphilis after three months. During clinical trials involving 49,038 patients treated with oral and parenteral ciprofloxacin, most adverse events were mild or moderate in severity, resolved shortly after discontinuation of the drug, and required no treatment. Ciprofloxacin was discontinued due to adverse events in 1% of orally treated patients. Common adverse events included nausea (3%), vomiting (1%), and rash (1%). Additional medically significant events occurred in less than 1% of patients and included: Body as a Whole: Headache, abdominal pain/discomfort, foot pain, pain in extremities, injection site reactions (for intravenous ciprofloxacin). Cardiovascular: Palpitations, atrial flutter, ventricular ectopy, syncope, hypertension, angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, cardiopulmonary arrest, cerebral thrombosis, phlebitis, tachycardia, migraine, hypotension. Central Nervous System: Restlessness, dizziness, lightheadedness, insomnia, nightmares, hallucinations, manic reactions, irritability, tremor, ataxia, convulsive seizures (including status epilepticus), grand mal convulsions, lethargy, drowsiness, weakness, malaise, anorexia, phobias, depersonalization, depression (potentially culminating in self-injurious behavior, such as suicidal ideation or attempts), paresthesia, abnormal gait. Gastrointestinal: Painful oral mucosa, oral candidiasis, dysphagia, intestinal perforation, gastrointestinal bleeding, cholestatic jaundice, hepatitis. Hemic/Lymphatic: Lymphadenopathy, petechiae. Metabolic/Nutritional: Increased amylase, increased lipase, hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia. Musculoskeletal: Arthralgia or back pain, joint stiffness, achiness, neck or chest pain, gout flare-ups, muscle weakness. Renal/Urogenital: Interstitial nephritis, nephritis, renal failure, polyuria, urinary retention, urethral bleeding, vaginitis, acidosis, breast pain. Respiratory: Dyspnea, epistaxis, laryngeal or pulmonary edema, hiccups, hemoptysis, bronchospasm, pulmonary embolism. Skin/Hypersensitivity: Allergic reactions, pruritus, urticaria, photosensitivity/phototoxicity reactions, flushing, fever, chills, angioedema, edema of the face, neck, lips, conjunctivae, or hands, cutaneous candidiasis, hyperpigmentation, erythema nodosum, sweating. Special Senses: Blurred vision, disturbed vision (e.g., changes in color perception, overbrightness of lights), decreased visual acuity, diplopia, eye pain, tinnitus, hearing loss, bad taste, chromatopsia. In some cases, nausea, vomiting, tremor, irritability, or palpitations were attributed to elevated serum levels of theophylline, possibly due to drug interactions with ciprofloxacin. In randomized, double-blind controlled clinical trials comparing ciprofloxacin tablets (500 mg BID) to cefuroxime axetil (250–500 mg BID) and clarithromycin (500 mg BID) in patients with respiratory tract infections, ciprofloxacin demonstrated a central nervous system adverse event profile comparable to the control drugs. Ciprofloxacin, administered intravenously and/or orally, was compared to a cephalosporin for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI) or pyelonephritis in pediatric patients aged 1 to 17 years (mean age 6 ± 4 years). The trial, conducted in multiple countries, assessed musculoskeletal and neurological safety within six weeks of therapy and through one year of follow-up in 335 ciprofloxacin-treated and 349 comparator-treated patients. An Independent Pediatric Safety Committee (IPSC) reviewed all cases of musculoskeletal adverse events, including conditions such as arthralgia, abnormal gait, joint sprains, leg pain, back pain, arthrosis, bone pain, myalgia, and decreased range of motion in joints. Affected joints included the knee, elbow, ankle, hip, wrist, and shoulder. Musculoskeletal events occurred in 3% of ciprofloxacin-treated patients compared to 6% of comparator-treated patients. Most events were mild or moderate in intensity and resolved within 30 days of treatment cessation. Radiological evaluations were not routinely used to confirm resolution. These events occurred more frequently in ciprofloxacin-treated patients, regardless of whether they received intravenous or oral therapy.
